title: A screen fast
hookLine: fasting from screens as a modern penance
tomorrow: can loving one person deeply make your heart smaller?

cards: A digital detox usually starts with an announcement. A goodbye post. A story with a countdown.
Logging off, see you in a week. Now set that next to the fasting instructions Jesus gives in Matthew, which sound backwards.
Don't look gloomy, he says, like the ones who make their faces sad so everyone can see they're fasting. Instead, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "anoint thy head, and wash thy face." Fix your hair.
Look ordinary. Why would a fast need a face wash?

teach.h: THE FACE WASH HIDES THE FAST.
teach.b: The next verse solves it. Wash your face so that you don't look like you're fasting to people, but only to your Father, who sees in secret. The face wash hides the fast.

A fast that needs an audience has quietly changed who it's for. The applause becomes the reward, and the reward is used up right there. So in Matthew, fasting is a private turn toward God, not a performance of being good.

That's close to what the Church means by penance: not a punishment you serve, but turning back toward God, and making a little room in your life by going without something you would normally reach for.
Church law calls every Friday of the year, and the whole of Lent, days of penance. And it lets the bishops of each country set other forms of penance alongside fasting and abstinence from meat.
So some Catholics today choose a screen fast: an evening, a Friday, a weekend with the phone in a drawer. The old logic still holds. Going without food leaves a hunger you can turn toward God.
Going without the scroll leaves a silence, and an empty hand, and an evening that suddenly has room in it for the people at the table. And the face wash still applies.
No countdown post. The people who need to know, know. Everyone else just meets someone a little more present.

how: Catholics keep Fridays and Lent as days of penance, by fasting, by abstaining from meat or by another penance their bishops allow; some choose time away from screens as that penance.

games.q: you've started a screen-free Sunday night. a friend texts Monday: "where were you??" going by Matthew 6, what fits?
o: tell her plainly you were offline Sunday, no big speech.
post a story explaining the fast so nobody else worries.
make up an excuse so no one ever finds out you're fasting.
games.why: Matthew's face wash isn't lying; it's not making a show. a plain answer to a friend is honest, and the fast stays between you and God.

practice: Make a small plan. Pick one evening this week for a screen fast. Name the thing most likely to break it: the reflex to check, a group chat, boredom at nine o'clock.
Then decide one move for that moment, like a phone in another room or a book on the couch, and keep the plan between you and God.

wordCard.voice: A screen fast. Going without the phone for a set time, as a quiet penance, to make room. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a fast. the Church's old word for going without, as a turn toward God.

carryVoice: Keep this one: fast from screens, with a washed face and no countdown post. Off you go.
